description.narrative: Denna insats genom Världsbankens TF syftar till att bidra till att bygga och stärka socialt skydd och arbetsmarknadssystem i utvecklingsländerna, nämligen i Afrika. Insatsen avser system för social trygghet, socialförsäkring och arbetsmarknadsprogram. Det övergripande målet är att förbättra de fattigas motståndskraft mot oväntade katastrofer och kriser.

The proposed intervention is relevant to the broader objective of fighting poverty and strengthening of institutions in order to ensure a better and rapid response to crisis and emergencies. The programme will also assist in building up efficient social protection and labor systems to help the poor and vulnerable and to mitigate the harmful effects of crises in a coherent manner.

The Rapid Social Response Multi-donor Trust Fund (RSR-MDTF) was designed as a response to meet the effects of the financial crises in 2008-2009 and a tool to further enhance the implementation of the Social Protection and Jobs sector strategy also known as the SPJ Compass 2012-2022. It had renewed interest in 2019-2020 and a parallel Trust Fund was established under an RSR Adaptive Umbrella Trust Fund (RSR-ADSP) as a response to the COVID-19 crisis. The RSR-MDTF/RSR-ADSP (RSR) have thematic windows for example a classical window and thematic windows for gender, youth and food security.
The World Bank reports that the RSR has: • leveraged over US$8.5 billion of International Development Association (IDA) and US$1.7 billion of International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) operations and a matching $7 billion in Government financed SPJ programs and other domestic resource mobilization - altogether $17.2 billion, • Reached over 175 million poor and vulnerable people increasingly women. Helped 99 countries enhance the capacity of social protection and jobs systems, • Facilitated new partnerships and promoted global knowledge exchanges such as the South-South Learning Forum and numerous regional and sub-regional Communities of Practice on social protection and jobs issues, • Helped develop six Inter-Agency Social Protection Assessment (ISPA) tools. Out of 69 ISPA applications, half of them are supported by RSR funding, • improved the ASPIRE (Atlas of Social Protection Indicators of Resilience and Equity) that now includes performance indicators of social protection program based on 328 surveys from 124 countries.
RSR Phase 2 (2012-2024) financed by Sida: supported countries through new innovative, catalytic windows aimed at increasing the adaptability of social protection systems during crisis and in particularly high impact areas such as nutrition, disaster risk management, fragility, youth empowerment, gender-smart social protection, digital economy and artificial intelligence. The fund provided small, averaging US$356,000, but highly catalytic funding and paved the way for larger World Bank supported operations. In total RSR awarded 149.8 million USD in 420 grants, with nearly US$150 million in funding, allocated through 21 competitive calls for proposals.
From 2013 to 2018, RSR expanded its scope: supporting country reforms, piloting innovations, and advancing policies that empowered vulnerable populations beyond immediate crisis response. Women, migrants, people with disabilities, and displaced communities remained central to this agenda.
In 2014, RSR began addressing risk head-on, supporting countries to strengthen disaster preparedness and integrate resilience into social protection systems to deliver services more effectively in crises. RSRs approach emphasized practical design parameters to guide disaster-responsive social protection: establish disaster financing mechanisms in advance, foster inter-agency coordination, invest early in delivery systems, and build flexibility into programs. These principles applied across dozens of grants enabled countries to act faster and more effectively in times of crisis. Equally important was the focus on reliable data systems and strong institutional capacity, which ensured programs could scale quickly and deliver targeted support when and where it mattered most. The RSR-ADSP also supports efforts to expand access and opportunities to strengthen household resilience, develop sustainable livelihoods, and improve productivity to foster human capital and a durable escape from poverty for all.
The RSR-ADSP has been instrumental in addressing emerging concerns and helping the Bank and clients respond to new crises. Beginning with Round 18 in 2020, when Sida decided to add financing to the fund, the RSR-ADSP pivoted to support clients and teams adapt social protection and safety net programs to deal with the COVID-19 crisis where the World bank estimates that 49 million people were pushed into extreme poverty.
RSR worked to overcome structural barriers to economic inclusion so that more people can access jobs, services, and opportunities to break the cycle of poverty. At the same time, RSR showed that clients respond most to credible evidence and demonstration, and that true partnerships go beyond funding to build trust, spark innovation, and sustain impact. Also, RSR grants have also enabled greater dialogue with clients, provided analytical and diagnostic information to strengthen program design, supported teams to innovate and take risks with new ideas, and financed the development of new tools and other public goods that have enhanced social protection and labor programming around the world.
Links to Sida's bilateral portfolio
As mentioned above the RSR-ADSP provides small but highly catalytic financing for innovative activities that often pave the way for larger World Bank supported operations and where some have direct or indirect links to Sida financed bilateral assistance. A few examples are listed below:
In Liberia, an RSR grant supported the design and roll-out of a national social registry integrated with the IDA-backed safety net project. The initiative delivered concrete results: alternative approaches for a nationwide database, a new management information system to eliminate duplication and inefficiencies, and a harmonized targeting mechanism to support unified program delivery. These efforts shaped the Liberia Social Safety Nets Project, a five-year, $10 million IDA operation providing income support to the poorest and most food-insecure households. The program is co-financed by Sida.
An RSR-supported study in Zambia identified ways to adapt social protection programs to reduce gender based violence (GBV) risks and the World Banks Girls Education and Women's Empowerment and Livelihoods (GEWEL) and Supporting Women's Livelihoods (SWL) have mobilized male champions, school-based campaigns, and traditional leaders to confront GBV and promote equitable relationships. In addition in Zambia and Tanzania, efforts to improve grievance redress mechanisms, update referral pathways, and increase survivor confidentiality have begun to close the gap. Sida have co-financed GEWEL in Zambia and the social protection development in Tanzania.
Another example is Afghanistan where ultra-poor households, particularly women-headed households facing socioeconomic challenges and high vulnerability received a multi-dimensional economic inclusion package, using a tailored Poverty Graduation approach.
Knowledge products for Policy and Practice
Over the years, a wide range of reports, tool-kits, and policy briefs have advanced knowledge across countries. By collecting lessons from research, operational experience, and global evidence, these resources provide a robust evidence base that helps policymakers and practitioners design stronger programs and build social protection systems that are more inclusive, resilient, and adaptive. Today there are more than 450 publicly available reports, tool-kits, working papers, and books, and the creation of dozens of knowledge platforms, partnerships, and learning events. Some key documents are listed below: - The 1.5 Billion People Question: Food, Vouchers, or Cash Transfers?, 2017 - The Future of Work in Africa, 2020 - Investing in Early Childhood Development, 2015 - Exploring Universal Basic Income: A Guide to Navigating Concepts, Evidence, and Practices, 2020 - Adaptive Social Protection (ASP)a proactive approach that strengthens household resilience before a shock and improves recovery afterward, 2020 - The Safety First: How to Leverage Safety Nets to Prevent Gender-Based Violence toolkit was launched in June 2021 - Insights and Lessons from Interventions in Settings of Fragility, Conflict, and Violence, 2024
Global Platforms
The RSR has played a catalytic role in advancing many global social protection initiatives. By funding analytical work, piloting innovations, and supporting country operations, RSR has helped generate the data, evidence, and operational models that underpin platforms such as ASPIRE, Solutions for youth employment (S4YE), Universal Social Protection 2030 (USP2030), and Social Protection Inter Agency Cooperation - Board (SPIAC-B).
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
